title: Rabbi Yosef Bekhor Shor: A Biographical and Intellectual Portrait of a 12th-Century Exegete

Rabbi Yosef Bekhor Shor: A Biographical and Intellectual Portrait of a 12th-Century Exegete
1. Introduction: Rabbi Yosef Bekhor Shor's Place in the World of Exegesis
Rabbi Yosef Bekhor Shor was a central and important figure in the school of peshat (plain-sense) exegesis that flourished in Northern France during the 12th century. He stands as a unique and significant link in the historical chain of biblical exegesis, between the foundational work of Rashi and the rise of the Tosafists. His contribution to biblical exegesis was marked by loyalty to the French tradition of adherence to peshat, combined with linguistic, literary and psychological tools that gave his commentaries depth and originality.
This document is intended to present a comprehensive portrait of the life and work of R. Yosef Bekhor Shor. We will sketch the few known facts of his life, analyse the basic features of his exegetical method, and place him within the rich historical and intellectual context of his time. To assess the magnitude of his contribution properly, it is first necessary to understand the vibrant intellectual environment in which he grew up, an environment that shaped the ways of thinking and creating of all the sages of Ashkenaz.
2. The Historical and Intellectual Background: Ashkenazi Jewry in the 12th Century
Understanding the context of the 12th century in Northern French Jewry is key to assessing the work of any exegete active there. The intellectual atmosphere, marked by the tension between peshat exegesis and derash (homiletical) exegesis; the religious disputations with Christianity, which posed new challenges to Jewish thought; and the relatively stable socio-economic situation of the communities – all these together shaped the world of the sages and directly influenced the exegetical methods they developed.
2.1. The Rise of Peshat Exegesis in Northern France
At the heart of the intellectual revolution in medieval France stood the rise of the peshat approach – the striving to understand Scripture according to the "literal, simple, clear, natural and direct" meaning of the text. This approach developed as a reaction against the dominance of derash exegesis, which tended to distance the text from its primary meaning. Several factors combined to give rise to the peshat school:
The development of Hebrew grammar: The work of the Masoretes, which reached its peak in the ninth century, laid the foundations for the systematic study of biblical language and provided essential tools for exegesis based on linguistic subtleties.
The interreligious disputation: The intellectual confrontation with Christianity, which emphasised allegorical interpretations in order to ground its beliefs, compelled the Jewish sages to sharpen their literal interpretations and to defend the plain meaning of Scripture.
The influence of Rashi: Rashi (R. Shlomo Yitzchaki), the greatest of the French exegetes, paved the way for generations of exegetes after him. Although he incorporated many midrashim into his commentary, he set peshat as a guiding principle and provided an exegetical model that deeply influenced his students, his grandsons (Rashbam and Rabbenu Tam), and the entire school.
2.2. The Scholarly Atmosphere in Ashkenaz
In the first half of the 12th century, the Jews of France enjoyed relative economic and social stability, which allowed spiritual life and Torah study to flourish. Jewish communities held fields and vineyards, enjoyed internal autonomy and managed their affairs independently. This period, which preceded the Second Crusade, allowed the sages to devote their time to in-depth study.
Nevertheless, it is important to distinguish between the Ashkenazi linguistic school and the Sephardi one. Whereas the sages of Sepharad, influenced by the Muslim environment and the Arabic language, delved deeply into the study of grammar and philology, their colleagues in Ashkenaz focused mainly on halakhic and Talmudic inquiry. The study of language served them chiefly as an auxiliary tool for understanding Scripture and the Talmud, and not as an independent field of research. Within this vibrant intellectual world, marked by intensive Talmudic study and a growing striving to understand the plain sense of Scripture, R. Yosef Bekhor Shor grew and developed.
3. A Biographical Portrait and the Riddle of Identity
The biographical details known to us about R. Yosef Bekhor Shor are few and fragmentary. Like other sages of his generation, he left no autobiography, and the information about his life has been gathered mainly from his writings and from mentions in the literature of the period. This scarcity poses a significant challenge to scholars attempting to reconstruct the course of his life and his influences.
3.1. His Life and Early Influences
R. Yosef Bekhor Shor lived and worked in Northern France during the 12th century. According to scholars' conjecture, he was born around 1140. His epithet, "Bekhor Shor", derives from Moses' blessing of Joseph in the verse "His firstling bullock, majesty is his" (Bekhor shoro hadar lo; Deuteronomy 33:17), an epithet indicating glory and strength. His father's name is not known with certainty, but it may have been Yitzchak, and it was apparently from him that he received his early Torah education, as is hinted by a single mention of his father (without his name) in his commentary.
The central figure who influenced his intellectual formation was his teacher, Rabbenu Tam (R. Yaakov ben Meir), Rashi's grandson and one of the greatest of the Tosafists. Rabbenu Tam's esteem for him was great, as attested by the epithet he gave him: "wise and beyond his years, my colleague, Rabbi Yosef".
3.2. The Scholarly Question: R. Yosef Bekhor Shor and R. Yosef of Orléans
One of the central questions in the study of his figure is the question of his identity: is R. Yosef Bekhor Shor the same person mentioned in the Tosafot to the Talmud as "Rabbi Yosef of Orléans"? The scholarly debate on this question has continued for many years, and arguments have been raised on both sides:
Arguments supporting separation: Certain scholars have pointed out that medieval exegetical compilations, such as "Pa'aneach Raza", quote interpretations in the name of R. Yosef of Orléans alongside interpretations in the name of R. Yosef Bekhor Shor. This fact suggests that the compilers regarded them as two separate figures.
Arguments supporting identification: On the other hand, most scholars point to significant evidence supporting the identification of the two figures. For example, an interpretation that appears in the Tosafot to tractate Shabbat in the name of R. Yosef of Orléans appears identically in Bekhor Shor's commentary on the Book of Exodus. Prominent scholars such as Gross, Poznanski and Urbach supported this identification, explaining that the absence of certain interpretations attributed to R. Yosef of Orléans from Bekhor Shor's manuscript is not conclusive evidence. Bekhor Shor's commentary survived in a single manuscript (the Munich manuscript), and there is no knowing whether it is complete.
Today, the view accepted by most scholars, and the one adopted in this source, is that this is indeed the same person. Beyond the biographical details, Bekhor Shor's main contribution lies in his exegetical work and his unique approach.
4. Basic Features of His Exegetical Method
R. Yosef Bekhor Shor positioned himself as an exegete who combined loyalty to the French exegetical tradition with original insights and unique analytical tools. He worked at the seam between Rashi and the Tosafists, and his commentary can be seen as an attempt to enrich peshat exegesis with tools that were not common before him. His approach rests on a number of basic principles that shape the character of the entire commentary.
4.1. Adherence to Peshat and Opposition to Allegory
Bekhor Shor's commitment to peshat was absolute. He advocated simplicity in faith and in opinion, and sharply opposed any allegorical or symbolic interpretation that might empty the commandments of their practical and concrete meaning. He saw in such an approach a danger to faith and to the proper observance of the commandments. His sharpest criticism was directed against those who interpret the commandment of mezuzah as a mere parable, or the commandment of covering the blood as a hygienic measure for keeping courtyards clean. Of such exegetes he declared emphatically that "their books deserve to be burned". Scholars conjecture that the spearhead of this criticism was directed mainly against Christian exegetes, who tended to interpret the Torah allegorically in order to ground their theological conceptions.
4.2. Psychological Sense and Insights into Biblical Characters
One of the prominent and distinctive features of Bekhor Shor is his psychological ability to penetrate the souls of biblical characters and to uncover their motives. This trait clearly distinguishes him from other exegetes in Northern France, who focused mainly on textual and linguistic questions. Bekhor Shor tried to understand "why and how" the characters acted as they did.
Two central examples illustrate his approach:
Cain and Abel: Bekhor Shor explains Cain's motives for the murder not as pure evil, but as a deep distress that stemmed from a sense of rejection after God preferred Abel's offering. After his conversation with God, he exploited Abel's innocence, pretended to have made peace with him, and only then, when they were in the field and Abel was not suspicious, killed him. This is a psychological analysis of an act driven by jealousy, insult and cunning.
Eliezer and Rebekah: Why did Abraham's servant choose to test Rebekah by the well and not in her home? Bekhor Shor explains this with a sharp psychological insight: had the test been held in her home, she might have passed it out of obedience to her parents, and not out of genuine character traits of kindness and generosity. The test outside the home, in the public space and without supervision, ensured that her behaviour would reflect her true personality.
4.3. Attitude to the World of His Time
Unlike other exegetes, Bekhor Shor's commentary does not abound in geographical or historical explanations or in descriptions of daily life. Nevertheless, in a few places he alludes to contemporary customs in order to clarify Scripture. For example, he explains the verse "and you shall break his yoke from off your neck" as an expression of a vassal's rebellion against his lord in the feudal system. Elsewhere, he mentions the custom of princes who sealed agreements by means of their glove (gauntlet) in order to explain a biblical expression. These rare mentions offer a glimpse into his world, but they are not a central feature of his commentary.
5. A Methodological Analysis of the Exegetical Tools
Although he was not a linguist or grammarian in the professional sense, as the sages of Sepharad were, R. Yosef Bekhor Shor incorporated sophisticated linguistic and literary analyses into his commentary. He did not write books on grammar, but his remarks, woven throughout his commentary, attest to a high awareness of the structure of the Hebrew language and to a systematic use of these tools to ground his peshat interpretations.
5.1. Linguistic and Grammatical Foundations
Bekhor Shor dealt with a wide range of grammatical questions, clarifying difficulties in the text by means of them:
Distinguishing between tenses and verb patterns: He discusses cases in which a verb in the future form carries the meaning of the present or of the imperative, thereby resolving apparent contradictions in the text.
Morphological homonyms: He identified words with identical spelling but different meanings. The prominent example is the word "ki", to which he ascribes four different meanings: "if", "lest", "but" and "because".
Grammatical gender and number: He analysed cases of apparent grammatical disagreement between a noun and an adjective or between masculine and feminine, and proposed rules explaining these phenomena in biblical language.
5.2. Etymological Interpretation
Bekhor Shor used a variety of etymological methods to clarify the meaning of difficult or obscure words:
Similarity of sound: He linked words of similar sound in order to infer their meaning. For example, he connects the word "kivrat" (eretz) to the word "kabir" (mighty, great), and explains that a great distance is meant.
Comparison with Scripture: He interpreted words on the basis of similar usage elsewhere in Scripture. For example, he interprets the verb "vayatzel" ("rescued") in the sense of "separation", on the basis of the verse "and I will take (ve-atzalti) of the spirit which is upon you".
Use of rabbinic language: At times he relies on the language of the Sages. For example, he interprets the word "avrekh" as a compound of the words "av" ("father", in wisdom) and "rakh" ("tender", in years), as it appears in the Midrash.
5.3. Semantic and Syntactic Analysis
His analytical abilities also found expression in analysing meaning according to context (semantics) and in solving problems of sentence structure (syntax).
Semantics: He stressed how the context of the sentence determines the meaning of a word. For example, he interprets the word "shevet" (Genesis 49:10) not as a physical rod but as "rule" or "government".
Syntax (ambiguous subject): He discusses complex syntactic structures, as expressed in the question of the identity of the subject in the sentence "and he counted it to him as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6). Like Ramban, Bekhor Shor argues that it was Abraham who counted God's promise to Him as an act of righteousness. He thereby rejects on rational grounds the alternative interpretation (found in Rashi), according to which it was God who counted Abraham's faith to him as righteousness. His reasoning is that faith in God is a self-evident act, and it should not be seen as a unique act deserving a special reward of righteousness.
Syntax (elliptical sentences): Bekhor Shor identified and supplied verbs or nouns that were missing from biblical sentences in order to clarify their meaning, a technique that attests to a deep understanding of the structure of the Hebrew sentence.
5.4. Literary and Stylistic Features
Bekhor Shor displayed an awareness of literary structures and stylistic devices in the biblical text, and saw in them a key to understanding the intent of Scripture.
Recurring themes: He explained why the count of the Children of Israel appears at the beginning of the Book of Exodus, although it had already appeared at the end of the Book of Genesis. In his view, the repetition is meant to stress that the Children of Israel are the central subject of the new book.
Identifying parallel events: He identified parallel stories in different books and at times argued that they refer to the same event. For example, he argued that the story of the quails in the Book of Exodus and the parallel story in the Book of Numbers describe a single event.
Use of hermeneutical rules: He used Talmudic rules of interpretation, such as "a general statement followed by an action" or "a matter learned from its context", in order to explain the structure of the text and its logical sequence.
6. Scholarly Discourse and Mutual Influences
R. Yosef Bekhor Shor did not work in a vacuum. He was part of an extensive intellectual network of the sages of Northern France and conducted a dialogue, direct or indirect, with his contemporaries and his predecessors. An analysis of his ties with other sages reveals the sources of influence on his work, and at the same time highlights its originality and unique contribution.
6.1. Rabbenu Tam: Teacher and Student
The relationship between Bekhor Shor and his teacher, Rabbenu Tam, was one of mutual respect and esteem. Although Bekhor Shor does not mention his teacher by name in his commentary on the Torah, in a question he addressed to him elsewhere he opens with words attesting to his humility and to the respect he felt for him: "The least of his students and attendants...". A possible influence of Rabbenu Tam on his student can be identified, mainly in their shared interest in the subtleties of language and grammar. This finds expression, for example, in a comparison of their interpretations of words such as "bilti" or of the expression "ein Yaakov".
6.2. The Connection to Rashbam
The connection between Bekhor Shor's commentary and that of Rashbam (R. Shmuel ben Meir, Rashi's grandson) is more complex. Bekhor Shor mentions Rashbam by name several times, and frequently offers interpretations very similar to his, at times even without mentioning his name. This makes it difficult to determine the extent of direct influence. It is possible that in many cases both reached similar conclusions independently, or relied on a shared exegetical tradition. In one interesting case, Bekhor Shor quotes an interpretation he heard from Rashbam on the verse "And He took off their chariot wheels" (Exodus 14:25), but the version he cites differs from the version appearing in Rashbam's own commentary, which points to oral transmission or to selective memory.
6.3. The Dialogue with Ibn Ezra
The scholarly discussion of the connection between Bekhor Shor and R. Abraham ibn Ezra is especially fascinating. Ibn Ezra, a man of Sepharad, visited France and stayed there, and there is evidence of ties he maintained with the Tosafists. An examination of their commentaries reveals a marked similarity on many subjects: both interpret the word "toledot" as "events", or identify "the place of Shechem" as a future site not yet built. These and many other similarities point to a high probability of mutual influence, whether through direct encounter or through intermediaries. Nevertheless, this cannot be proven unequivocally, and the possibility that each reached his conclusions independently remains open.
7. Legacy and Lasting Influence: The Paradox of Circulation
The legacy of R. Yosef Bekhor Shor presents a fascinating paradox. On the one hand, his commentary on the Torah survived in only a single manuscript and did not achieve wide circulation as an independent work. On the other hand, it became a central source of influence for the later generations of the Tosafists, who quoted it extensively in their compilations.
The reason why only one manuscript survived is unclear, but it may be conjectured that the reason is connected to its success. It is possible that his interpretations were incorporated so intensively into the later compilations that there was no longer any practical need to copy his work separately. His influence is clearly evident in exegetical compilations such as "Da'at Zekenim", "Hadar Zekenim" and **"Hizkuni"**. In these compilations he is quoted sometimes by name and sometimes anonymously, and it was they that made his thought common property.
The field in which his influence was greatest is semantic exegesis – the analysis of the meaning of words according to their context. This field, which was the main focus of his expertise, is the one that penetrated deeply into the study hall of the Tosafists and left its mark on Ashkenazi exegesis for generations. Thus, his place in the history of exegesis far exceeds the limited circulation of the single manuscript that remains of his work.
8. Summary: The Contribution of R. Yosef Bekhor Shor to the World of Biblical Exegesis
Rabbi Yosef Bekhor Shor was a distinct peshat exegete, who enriched the Northern French tradition of the 12th century with a dimension of analytical depth. He was not content with offering a literal interpretation, but strove to ground it by means of sophisticated linguistic, literary and psychological tools. In this way, he bridged the world of peshat of Rashi and Rashbam and the in-depth analysis of the Tosafists.
His importance lies in his ability to show how the language of Scripture can be analysed in depth, how the motives of the characters can be uncovered, and how the literary structures of the text can be understood, all while adhering uncompromisingly to the plain meaning. He deeply influenced the following generations of Ashkenazi exegetes, who made his interpretations an inseparable part of their exegetical treasury. Despite the limited circulation of his independent writings, R. Yosef Bekhor Shor stands as one of the pillars of medieval peshat exegesis, and his voice continues to resonate in the exegetical study hall to this day.

Bekhor Shor displayed an awareness of literary structures and stylistic devices in the biblical text, and saw in them a key to understanding the intent of Scripture.
Recurring themes: He explained why the count of the Children of Israel appears at the beginning of the Book of Exodus, although it had already appeared at the end of the Book of Genesis. In his view, the repetition is meant to stress that the Children of Israel are the central subject of the new book.
Identifying parallel events: He identified parallel stories in different books and at times argued that they refer to the same event. For example, he argued that the story of the quails in the Book of Exodus and the parallel story in the Book of Numbers describe a single event.
Use of hermeneutical rules: He used Talmudic rules of interpretation, such as "a general statement followed by an action" or "a matter learned from its context", in order to explain the structure of the text and its logical sequence.
6. Scholarly Discourse and Mutual Influences
R. Yosef Bekhor Shor did not work in a vacuum. He was part of an extensive intellectual network of the sages of Northern France and conducted a dialogue, direct or indirect, with his contemporaries and his predecessors. An analysis of his ties with other sages reveals the sources of influence on his work, and at the same time highlights its originality and unique contribution.
6.1. Rabbenu Tam: Teacher and Student
The relationship between Bekhor Shor and his teacher, Rabbenu Tam, was one of mutual respect and esteem. Although Bekhor Shor does not mention his teacher by name in his commentary on the Torah, in a question he addressed to him elsewhere he opens with words attesting to his humility and to the respect he felt for him: "The least of his students and attendants...". A possible influence of Rabbenu Tam on his student can be identified, mainly in their shared interest in the subtleties of language and grammar. This finds expression, for example, in a comparison of their interpretations of words such as "bilti" or of the expression "ein Yaakov".
6.2. The Connection to Rashbam
The connection between Bekhor Shor's commentary and that of Rashbam (R. Shmuel ben Meir, Rashi's grandson) is more complex. Bekhor Shor mentions Rashbam by name several times, and frequently offers interpretations very similar to his, at times even without mentioning his name. This makes it difficult to determine the extent of direct influence. It is possible that in many cases both reached similar conclusions independently, or relied on a shared exegetical tradition. In one interesting case, Bekhor Shor quotes an interpretation he heard from Rashbam on the verse "And He took off their chariot wheels" (Exodus 14:25), but the version he cites differs from the version appearing in Rashbam's own commentary, which points to oral transmission or to selective memory.
6.3. The Dialogue with Ibn Ezra
The scholarly discussion of the connection between Bekhor Shor and R. Abraham ibn Ezra is especially fascinating. Ibn Ezra, a man of Sepharad, visited France and stayed there, and there is evidence of ties he maintained with the Tosafists. An examination of their commentaries reveals a marked similarity on many subjects: both interpret the word "toledot" as "events", or identify "the place of Shechem" as a future site not yet built. These and many other similarities point to a high probability of mutual influence, whether through direct encounter or through intermediaries. Nevertheless, this cannot be proven unequivocally, and the possibility that each reached his conclusions independently remains open.
7. Legacy and Lasting Influence: The Paradox of Circulation
The legacy of R. Yosef Bekhor Shor presents a fascinating paradox. On the one hand, his commentary on the Torah survived in only a single manuscript and did not achieve wide circulation as an independent work. On the other hand, it became a central source of influence for the later generations of the Tosafists, who quoted it extensively in their compilations.
The reason why only one manuscript survived is unclear, but it may be conjectured that the reason is connected to its success. It is possible that his interpretations were incorporated so intensively into the later compilations that there was no longer any practical need to copy his work separately. His influence is clearly evident in exegetical compilations such as "Da'at Zekenim", "Hadar Zekenim" and **"Hizkuni"**. In these compilations he is quoted sometimes by name and sometimes anonymously, and it was they that made his thought common property.
The field in which his influence was greatest is semantic exegesis – the analysis of the meaning of words according to their context. This field, which was the main focus of his expertise, is the one that penetrated deeply into the study hall of the Tosafists and left its mark on Ashkenazi exegesis for generations. Thus, his place in the history of exegesis far exceeds the limited circulation of the single manuscript that remains of his work.
8. Summary: The Contribution of R. Yosef Bekhor Shor to the World of Biblical Exegesis
Rabbi Yosef Bekhor Shor was a distinct peshat exegete, who enriched the Northern French tradition of the 12th century with a dimension of analytical depth. He was not content with offering a literal interpretation, but strove to ground it by means of sophisticated linguistic, literary and psychological tools. In this way, he bridged the world of peshat of Rashi and Rashbam and the in-depth analysis of the Tosafists.
His importance lies in his ability to show how the language of Scripture can be analysed in depth, how the motives of the characters can be uncovered, and how the literary structures of the text can be understood, all while adhering uncompromisingly to the plain meaning. He deeply influenced the following generations of Ashkenazi exegetes, who made his interpretations an inseparable part of their exegetical treasury. Despite the limited circulation of his independent writings, R. Yosef Bekhor Shor stands as one of the pillars of medieval peshat exegesis, and his voice continues to resonate in the exegetical study hall to this day.
A Comparative Analysis: Styles of Polemic against the Trinity in the Commentaries of Rashi, Rashbam and R. Yosef Bekhor Shor
1. Introduction: Scripture as a Polemical Battlefield
In the High Middle Ages, the Jewish-Christian polemic was conducted around one central battleground: the Hebrew Bible, or the "Old Testament" in Christian terminology. This book was the only source accepted by both sides from which theological proofs could be adduced. Whereas the Christians sought to prove that doctrines such as the Trinity and the Virgin Birth are hinted at and even explicit in the verses of Scripture, the task of the Jewish polemicists was to show how those very verses do not support this interpretation. Scripture, then, was not only a holy book, but an intellectual battlefield on which each side fought for the legitimacy of its faith.
Within this charged historical context worked three of the greatest exegetes of Northern France in the 11th and 12th centuries: Rashi, his grandson Rashbam, and their student R. Yosef Bekhor Shor. Their declared exegetical goal was to reach "the plain sense of Scripture" – the simple and logical meaning of the text. Nevertheless, the struggle over the meaning of these verses was not new to the Middle Ages. In fact, the rabbinic traditions about the Septuagint reveal an early awareness of the polemical potential latent in certain verses. According to these traditions, the seventy elders deliberately altered verses such as Genesis 1:26 from "na'aseh adam" ("Let us make man") to "I will make man", and Genesis 11:7 from "nerdah" ("let us go down") to "I will go down", precisely in order to prevent any interpretation implying a plurality of beings within the Godhead. The exegetes of Northern France, then, inherited an ancient battlefield, and when they approached verses that served as central Christian proofs, exegesis inevitably became a polemical response as well.
This document seeks to answer the following research question: how did the different exegetical styles of Rashi, Rashbam and Bekhor Shor lead to unique and distinct polemical approaches in dealing with Christian Trinitarian arguments (those concerning the Trinity)? This is done by examining their reliance on Talmudic sources, grammatical principles, and the degree of their direct confrontation with Christian doctrine.
To answer this question, we will first survey the exegetical-polemical approach of each of the sages, and then conduct an in-depth comparative analysis of the specific strategies they adopted.
2. A Survey of the Exegetes' Approaches
To understand the polemical style of each exegete, it is essential first to examine his overall exegetical approach. Despite their shared commitment to "peshat", each of them developed a unique methodology, which directly influenced the way he dealt with theological challenges. This commitment to peshat did not prevent them from developing clear polemical tendencies, even if not always explicit ones.
2.1. Rashi: Polemic Anchored in the Tradition of the Sages
Rashi's approach is characterised by consistent reliance on the sources of the Sages in order to reach "the plain sense of Scripture". For him, the words of the Sages are not merely a source of inspiration, but a central exegetical tool. In the polemical context, Rashi tends to rely especially on the passages on the minim (heretics) in the Talmud – specific discussions dealing with answering the claims of heretics – as the basis for his responses.
A clear example of this is his commentary on the verse in Genesis 1:26, "Let us make man in our image". Rashi, aware of the polemical challenge posed by the plural verb, adopts the explanation of R. Yochanan in the Talmud, according to which the Holy One, blessed be He, out of humility consulted with the "heavenly retinue" (the angels). In addition, he cites the Talmudic principle of "its refutation is beside it" – the fact that the next verse ("And God created man") uses the verb in the singular, thereby refuting from within the claim of a plurality of beings. Rashi's approach, then, is to integrate the polemical answer within a traditional exegetical framework, based on the authority of the Sages.
2.2. Rashbam: Polemic through Alternative Interpretation
Unlike his grandfather, Rashbam markedly reduces his reliance on Talmudic sources, preferring to offer exegetical solutions based on internal textual logic and on the context of the verses. His polemical strategy is indirect: he neutralises Trinitarian arguments by offering an alternative, coherent and simple explanation, which makes the Christian interpretation superfluous.
In his commentary on Genesis 1:26 ("Let us make man"), Rashbam resolves the problem by mentally adding one word: "And God said to His angels: Let us make man". In this way he clarifies to whom the words were said and removes any hint of plurality within the Godhead.
In his commentary on Genesis 19:24 ("Then the Lord rained... from the Lord"), Rashbam proposes that the first name of God refers to the angel Gabriel.
In this method, Rashbam does not confront the Christian claim directly. Nevertheless, his approach reveals a certain weakness; offering an exegetical alternative (such as identifying the name of God with Gabriel) opens the way for the Christian opponent simply to replace Gabriel with Jesus, thereby adopting the structure of Rashbam's argument for his own purposes.
2.3. R. Yosef Bekhor Shor: Direct and Incisive Polemic
Bekhor Shor represents an entirely different approach. He is not content with indirect solutions and tends to confront the Christian claim directly, at times using explicit expressions such as "an answer to the heretics". His innovative and unique strategy is the exposure of internal contradictions between the Christian interpretation proposed for a verse and Christian doctrine itself.
As an initial example, in his commentary on Genesis 1:26, after presenting traditional explanations, he turns directly to the Christian argument. He wonders how it is possible that "the Father" addresses "the Son" and the other beings with a command ("Let us make"), if all the beings of the Trinity are equal in status and in will. According to Christian logic itself, Bekhor Shor argues, the verse should have been phrased in the plural ("And they said"). In this way he turns the Christian proof on its head, using the principles of Christian theology to refute its interpretation.
This initial survey illustrates the essential differences between the approaches. We will now delve into a comparative analysis of the specific strategies each of them applied.
3. A Comparative Analysis of Polemical Strategies
The following analysis will focus on comparing the strategies of the three exegetes along three central axes: the manner of using the sources of the Sages, reliance on grammatical and stylistic logic, and the degree of direct confrontation with Christian doctrine.
3.1. Reliance on Talmudic Sources: Defensive versus Offensive Use
The difference between Rashi and Bekhor Shor in the manner of using Talmudic sources illustrates their different approaches well. Rashbam, as noted, generally avoids heavy reliance on these sources in the contexts under discussion.
3.2. Use of Grammatical and Stylistic Principles: Solution versus Refutation
Many verses that served as proofs of the Trinity were built on grammatical anomalies, such as the use of a plural verb with a singular noun ("Elohim"). The exegetes' ways of dealing with these phenomena reveal significant differences of approach.
Let us consider the verse in Genesis 19:24, "Then the Lord rained... from the Lord".
Rashi and Bekhor Shor: Both explain the repetition of the name of God as a biblical linguistic usage ("the manner of biblical language"), in which the name of the subject is repeated instead of using a pronoun (as in "the wives of Lamech"). This grammatical explanation resolves the exegetical difficulty and at the same time completely refutes the Christian claim of the existence of two beings.
Rashbam: Offers an alternative solution, according to which the first name of God is the angel Gabriel. This solution, as noted, does not refute the Christian interpretation hermetically, since the opponent can adopt the exegetical structure and replace Gabriel with Jesus.
In other verses, such as Genesis 20:13 ("God caused me to wander", with a plural verb), Rashi explains the phenomenon on the basis of a specific semantic-grammatical principle: the word "Elohim" is sometimes used in the sense of "lord", and in this sense too it can take a plural verb. By contrast, Bekhor Shor offers local and varied solutions: at one time the gods of the gentiles are meant, and at another God and His angels.
3.3. Direct Confrontation with Christian Doctrine: An Approach Unique to Bekhor Shor
This strategy is what most clearly distinguishes Bekhor Shor from his two predecessors, and it represents the height of his polemical sophistication. He is not content with refuting the Christian interpretation of the verse, but initiates an attack on the foundations of Christian doctrine by means of that very verse. His method can be characterised as a kind of theological reductio ad absurdum, in which he accepts for a moment his opponent's basic premise only in order to prove that it leads to an internal contradiction within his theological world.
The following are his main arguments exposing internal contradictions in the doctrine of the Trinity:
Genesis 1:26 ("Let us make man"): If all three beings of the Trinity are equal in status and in will, why does one being ("the Father") address the others with a command? It should have been written "And they said" (plural) and not "And he said" (singular).
Genesis 3:22 ("Behold, the man has become as one of us"): Bekhor Shor repeats the same argument, stressing that the singular verb "And the Lord said" at the beginning of the verse contradicts the idea of absolute equality between the beings.
Deuteronomy 6:5 ("And you shall love the Lord your God"): After the Christians claim that the three names of God in the preceding verse ("Hear, O Israel") hint at the Trinity, Bekhor Shor points out mockingly that here only two names are mentioned. He wonders sarcastically which being of the Trinity was "absent" from the command, and which of them need not be loved.
Genesis 18:2 and 19:1 (the three men and the two angels): Against the claim that the three men who visited Abraham are the Trinity, Bekhor Shor points out cynically that in the next chapter (19:1) only two angels arrive in Sodom. He asks where the third being, equal in status, disappeared to, thereby exposing the inconsistency of the proposed Christian narrative.
This strategy constitutes the strongest polemical argument, since it undermines the Christian interpretation from within its own theological world.
The essential differences in these strategies paint a clear picture of three different polemical approaches, which will be summarised below.
4. Summary and Conclusions: Three Exegetes, Three Polemical Approaches
The comparative analysis reveals how the shared commitment of Rashi, Rashbam and Bekhor Shor to "the plain sense of Scripture" gave rise to three distinct polemical approaches. Each approach stemmed from a different conception of "peshat": for Rashi, peshat is anchored in the tradition of the Sages; for Rashbam, it stems from the internal logic of the text; whereas for Bekhor Shor, it sometimes seems that the demands of peshat are subordinate to the urgent polemical goal. Each of them, in accordance with his exegetical methodology, developed a unique "polemical profile".
Rashi: Polemic as a Necessary By-product. For Rashi, polemic is not the goal, but an inevitable result of correct pedagogical exegesis. He does not go out to war; he teaches the text as it is, relying on the Sages, and the exegetical truth that follows from this is what wins the debate. The conservative polemicist uses the traditional tools to defend the tradition.
Rashbam: Polemic as Elegant Displacement. For Rashbam, polemic is an exercise in setting up an alternative. He does not refute the opponent's claim, but offers in its place an interpretation so coherent and simple that the Christian interpretation becomes cumbersome and superfluous. He is the indirect polemicist, who leaves the reader to draw the conclusion himself.
R. Yosef Bekhor Shor: Polemic as Intellectual Aggression. For Bekhor Shor, polemic is an initiated act of attack. He moves the battlefield into enemy territory and attacks Christian doctrine by means of its own internal inconsistency. He is the active polemicist, who does not hesitate to use sarcasm and sharp logical arguments as an exegetical weapon.
In conclusion, this comparison reveals not only different strategies of theological self-defence, but also the diversity, richness and vitality of the Northern French peshat school. It demonstrates the varied ways in which its exegetes coped with the intellectual challenges of their time. While Bekhor Shor's direct attacks are brilliant, it may be conjectured that Rashbam's subtle approach, which educates towards independent critical thinking, may have no less long-term influence.
Key Insights from the Commentary of R. Yosef Bekhor Shor: The "Double Stories" Approach
Executive Summary
This document summarises the unique exegetical approach of R. Yosef Bekhor Shor (Ribash), one of the prominent biblical exegetes of Northern France in the 12th century. Ribash, the student of Rashbam and Rabbenu Tam, was characterised by original, innovative and at times daring exegesis, which went beyond what was accepted in the Northern French peshat school.
His central innovation discussed in the source is his identification of "double stories" – cases in which Scripture apparently describes two different events, but in his view a single event described twice is meant. The central example analysed at length is the story of the Ma'apilim (Numbers 14) and the war against the Canaanite king of Arad at Hormah (Numbers 21), which in Ribash's view are not two separate events but a description of defeat and revenge in the same historical event.
Alongside this case, Ribash applies this principle to further cases, arguing that the stories of the quails, of bringing water out of the rock, and of the census of the Children of Israel likewise all took place only once, contrary to the first impression arising from the verses. The motives for this interpretation are explained in two ways: a tendency to reduce the number of miracles in Scripture, as Abraham Geiger proposed, and above all, a plain, close and precise reading of the biblical text, as emerges from Ribash's own commentaries.

Introduction: R. Yosef Bekhor Shor – An Original and Daring Exegete
R. Yosef Bekhor Shor (Ribash), who lived in Northern France between about 1130–1200, was one of the important biblical exegetes of his time. He belonged to the Northern French peshat school founded by Rashi and was the student of Rashbam and Rabbenu Tam. Although his commentary on the Torah did not achieve the popularity of Rashi's commentary, a study of it reveals an original and innovative exegete.
One of his greatest and most unique innovations is the identification of "double stories" in the Torah. Ribash was the first to point to cases in which the Torah appears to describe two separate events, but, as he argued, a single historical event is meant, told twice for various reasons.
Analysis of a Central Case: The Sin of the Ma'apilim and the War of Hormah
In the Book of Deuteronomy, Moses recounts historical events, among them the sin of the Ma'apilim, who tried to enter the Land of Israel after the sin of the spies, an event first described in the Book of Numbers. Ribash presents an in-depth and surprising analysis of this event, linking it to another story in the Book of Numbers.
Ribash's First Innovation: The Ma'apilim Were Not Killed
Contrary to the accepted view, Ribash argues that the Ma'apilim were not killed in their war against the Canaanites. He grounds his claim on linguistic precision in the text:
The expression in Deuteronomy 1:44: "as bees do" – Ribash interprets: "which sting a person here and there and do not kill him".
The expression in Numbers 14:45: "and smote them and beat them down" – Ribash interprets: "that they drove them off beaten and wounded, but did not kill them".
The absence of a count of the fallen: Ribash notes that the Torah does not give the number of the fallen in this war, unlike what is customary in descriptions of other wars, which strengthens the claim that there were no dead.
In his view, the Holy One, blessed be He, prevented their being killed "so that they would not boast over them and would not desecrate the Name of Heaven".
Ribash's Second Innovation: Uniting the Story of the Ma'apilim with the War of Arad
On the basis of the assumption that the Ma'apilim were not killed, Ribash presents his great and daring innovation, which unites two separate stories from the Book of Numbers:
The story of the Ma'apilim (Numbers 14:45): The defeat of the Ma'apilim and their pursuit "unto Hormah".
The war of the king of Arad (Numbers 21:1-3): A war is described in which the Canaanite king of Arad attacks Israel "and took some of them captive". Afterwards the Children of Israel vow a vow, defeat the Canaanite, destroy their cities, and call the place "Hormah".
Ribash proposes that these two stories in fact describe a single event in two stages:
"And it seems to me that this is 'And the Canaanite... heard... and took some of them captive' (Num. 21:1), but they did not kill any of them. And afterwards the Holy One, blessed be He, avenged them, as it is written, 'And Israel vowed a vow to the Lord' (Num. 21:2), 'and He delivered up the Canaanite... and the name of the place was called Hormah' (Num. 21:3) – both wars were at Hormah."
According to his interpretation:
The first battle, described in Numbers 21:1, is not a new event that took place in the fortieth year, but a further description of the war of the Ma'apilim that took place in the second year. In this battle, the Ma'apilim were beaten and taken captive, but were not killed.
The second battle, described in Numbers 21:2-3, is the revenge of the Children of Israel on the Canaanites for that defeat, which took place some 38 years later.
The name "Hormah" is mentioned in the early story of the Ma'apilim (Numbers 14) "after what was to come" – after the victory and the destruction (herem) that would come many years later.
Further Examples of the "Double Stories" Approach
Ribash applied the principle of exegetical unification to further prominent cases in the Torah:
There is a structural difference between the case of the Ma'apilim and the three other examples. Whereas in the stories of the quails, the water and the census Ribash argues that a later historical event was incorporated into the text at an earlier point, in the story of the Ma'apilim the situation is reversed: an early event is mentioned again at a later point for substantive reasons (to serve as background to the story of the revenge).
The Motives behind Ribash's Interpretation
The article presents two possible reasons that led Ribash to develop his daring exegetical approach:
A tendency to reduce miracles (Abraham Geiger's theory): The scholar Abraham Geiger argued that Ribash's aim was to diminish and reduce as far as possible the number of miraculous events in Scripture. The uniting of two miracle stories (the quails, the water from the rock) into a single event supports this claim. The article agrees that, in principle, Geiger's claim is correct.
A plain reading close to the text: This explanation is seen as more comprehensive, since it also explains the cases not connected with miracles (such as the Ma'apilim and the census). It seems that the main factor behind Ribash's innovations is a precise reading of the plain sense of the verses, which characterises his entire commentary on the Torah. Ribash himself attests to this method of his in one case when he writes: "kidmokhchei kera'ei" (as the verses prove).
